t: The letter names Paul as its writer
p: The letter says Paul wrote it. Whether he did is one of the most argued questions about the New Testament.
b: The letter opens with Paul's name and speaks in his voice to the end: a prisoner in Rome (1:8, 17), near death (4:6), with news and greetings from friends known from Acts. The church read it as Paul's last letter from the second century on. Since the 1800s many critical scholars have held that all three Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) were written after Paul's death by a follower, in Paul's name. The general case on both sides is set out on the topic page "The Pastoral Letters". 2 Timothy has its own case, because it is the most personal of the three: see the book page. This Plain translation follows the text as it stands and says "Paul" where the letter does.

p: "Christ" is the Greek for the Hebrew title Messiah, "anointed one". In Paul's letters it works almost as a name.
b: Christos is the Greek word for the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one": the king, priest or deliverer God anointed. By the time of Paul's letters it is often joined to Jesus' name as if it were a second name, and Paul, like the Pastoral Letters, likes the order "Christ Jesus" (eleven times in this short letter, against two of "Jesus Christ"). This site writes "Christ" in the letters and "the Messiah" where the Gospels and Acts use the word as a title. The King James Version often reads "Jesus Christ" in this letter (1:1, 1:10, 2:3, 4:1), because the later Greek manuscripts behind it often put the words in that order.

a: in keeping with the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus
t: An apostle for the sake of a promise
p: Paul's mission is tied to God's promise of life, which is found in Christ Jesus.
b: The Greek says Paul is an apostle kata "the promise of life". The preposition can mean "in keeping with" (his calling matches God's promise) or "for the sake of" (he is sent to announce it). Either way the note is struck that runs through the letter: a man facing death writes about life. "Life" comes back at once in 1:10, where Christ Jesus "has brought life and immortality out into the light", and the letter ends with the hope of "his kingdom in heaven" (4:18). Titus 1:2 begins in a similar way, with the hope of eternal life.

p: Paul calls Timothy his beloved child: a son in the faith, not by birth.
b: The Greek is agapeto tekno, "beloved child". Timothy's father was a Greek (Acts 16:1), and Paul is his father in the faith. Paul used the same words of him when he sent him to Corinth: "my beloved and faithful child in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 4:17). 1 Timothy 1:2 calls him a true child in the faith. The warmth of the title fits a letter that is full of longing (1:4; 4:9, 21) and reads like a father's last words to his son.

p: Paul's usual greeting is "grace and peace". The letters to Timothy add "mercy".
b: Most of Paul's letters open with "Grace to you and peace" (Romans 1:7; Ephesians 1:2). 1 and 2 Timothy add "mercy" in the middle, as 2 John 3 also does. "Mercy" (eleos) is the Greek Bible's usual word for God's faithful kindness to Israel, and "peace" stands for the Hebrew shalom. Paul ends Galatians with a Jewish-sounding wish, "May peace and mercy be on all who will walk by this rule" (Galatians 6:16). In this letter mercy comes back as a prayer for a friend (1:16, 18).

a: whom I serve with a clean conscience, as my forebears did
t: Paul and the God of his ancestors
p: Paul says he serves the same God his Jewish ancestors served. He does not see himself as having left Israel's faith.
b: The verb latreuo is the word for worship and service of God, used in the Greek Bible for Israel's worship. "From my forebears" means that Paul worships the God his Jewish ancestors worshiped. Acts gives Paul the same claim: "I serve our ancestors' God. I believe everything in line with the Law and everything written in the Prophets" (Acts 24:14), and "with a conscience that is good in every way" (Acts 23:1). Readers who stress Paul's Jewishness (the "Paul within Judaism" scholars) see here a man who never thought of himself as a convert to a new religion. Others note that the "clean conscience" is about Paul's sincerity, since elsewhere he calls his persecution of the church a sin he did in ignorance (1 Timothy 1:13).
r: Acts 24:14; Acts 23:1; Romans 1:9; Philippians 3:5-6; 1 Timothy 1:13; 1 Timothy 3:9

p: The letter does not say when Timothy cried. A parting, perhaps at Paul's arrest, is the usual guess.
b: Paul remembers Timothy's tears and longs to see him. The text does not say what parting is meant. Some think of a farewell like the one at Miletus, where the Ephesian elders "all broke into loud weeping" (Acts 20:37). Those who place the letter in a second imprisonment think of Paul's arrest after he had left Timothy in Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3). Readers who think a follower wrote the letter in Paul's name see the tears as part of the farewell scene the writer paints: an old teacher and a young successor. Either way, the letter's request is personal: come quickly (4:9, 21).

p: The Greek says Timothy's faith is "unhypocritical": not an act put on for others.
b: Anypokritos is built from the word for a stage actor (hypokrites, the source of "hypocrite") with a "not" in front. A faith "without play-acting" is genuine. Paul uses the word of love in Romans 12:9, and 1 Timothy 1:5 joins "a good conscience and a faith without pretense". The contrast in this letter is with the false teachers, who "hold on to the outward shape of godliness, but they have said no to its power" (3:5).

a: your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice
t: A faith handed down by women
p: Timothy's faith came through his grandmother and his mother. Acts says his mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek.
b: Lois and Eunice appear only here. Acts introduces Timothy at Lystra: "His mother was a Jewish believer, and his father a Greek" (Acts 16:1). The letter says the faith "made its home first" in them, then in Timothy, and that from childhood he knew "the holy writings" (3:15): taught, it seems, at home by the women of his family, since his father was not a Jew. Readers differ on whether "faith" here means their Jewish faith that later welcomed Jesus as Messiah, or their Christian faith from the time of Paul's first visit to Lystra (Acts 14:6-7). Either way, two Jewish women are named as the first teachers of one of the church's best-known leaders.

a: stir up the fire of God's gift again
p: The verb means to rekindle a fire, to stir the embers back to a blaze. It does not have to mean the fire had gone out.
b: Anazopyreo combines "again" or "up" with "keep a fire alive". It was used of stirring coals into flame. The image does not say that Timothy had lost the gift, only that a fire needs tending. The "gift" (charisma) is God's gracious gift given for service, the word Paul uses for the Spirit's gifts in Romans 12:6 and 1 Corinthians 12. The next verse says what kind of spirit it is: not cowardice but "power, love and clear thinking". The gift is linked to the laying on of hands, which the next note discusses.
orig: ἀναζωπυρεῖν τὸ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ (anazopyrein to charisma tou theou)

a: through the laying on of my hands
p: Here Paul laid hands on Timothy. In 1 Timothy 4:14 it was "the elders". The churches read this as ordination, or as a commissioning.
b: The Greek is dia tes epitheseos ton cheiron mou, "through the laying on of my hands": the gift came by means of the act, or together with it. Laying hands on someone with prayer is how the first churches set people apart for a task: the Seven (Acts 6:6), Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:3). 1 Timothy 4:14 uses a different preposition, meta, "with": the gift was given "through a prophecy, with the laying on of the elders' hands". There the prophecy is the means and the elders' hands go with it; here Paul's own hands are the means. Some readers think of one ceremony with Paul and the elders together; others of two different occasions. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican readers see here the rite of ordination handed on from the apostles; the Catholic Catechism cites 2 Timothy 1:6-7 in its teaching on holy orders (Catechism 1556). Many Protestants see a commissioning for a task, with prayer, without a sacrament. The "Where Christians differ" card on chapter 2 sets the views side by side.
orig: διὰ τῆς ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν μου (dia tes epitheseos ton cheiron mou)

p: Greek has no capital letters. "Spirit" here may be the Holy Spirit or a person's inner attitude.
b: The Greek pneuma can mean God's Spirit or a human spirit, a disposition. "God did not give us a spirit of cowardice" makes good sense either way. Many readers take the second half as the Holy Spirit himself, who brings "power, love and clear thinking", as in 1:14 ("the Holy Spirit, who has made his home in us"). Romans 8:15 has a similar contrast: not "a spirit of slavery" but the Spirit of adoption. The word for "cowardice" (deilia) is the shrinking back of a soldier, which fits the call to "suffer hard things" in 1:8 and 2:3.

p: The last word means self-control or sound judgment, the habit of thinking clearly under pressure.
b: Sophronismos belongs to the word family of sophrosyne, the Greek virtue of a sound and balanced mind and of self-control. The King James Version has "a sound mind"; other English versions say "self-control" or "self-discipline". The word can also mean bringing others to their senses. The Pastoral Letters often use this word family (1 Timothy 2:9, 15; Titus 2:2, 4-6, 12), so it is one of the virtues the letters ask of every church member.

p: Paul is a prisoner, in Rome (1:17), and expects to die (4:6). He calls himself the Lord's prisoner, not Caesar's.
b: The letter's setting is a Roman prison: Paul mentions his chain (1:16; 2:9), a first defense in court (4:16) and his coming death (4:6-8). Acts ends with two years of house arrest in Rome, with freedom to receive visitors (Acts 28:30-31). The tradition that Paul was freed, traveled again and was imprisoned a second time is found in Eusebius' Church History (2.22), who says Paul wrote this letter in that second imprisonment, and the earlier 1 Clement (chapter 5) says Paul reached "the extreme limit of the west" before he died. Readers who think the letter was written after Paul's death read these details as the writer's picture of Paul's last days. By saying "his" prisoner, Paul treats his chains as service to Christ, as in Ephesians 3:1.

a: Take your share of hardship with me
p: Paul uses a rare compound, "suffer-hardship-with", found in the New Testament only in this letter.
b: Synkakopatheo joins "with" to "suffer hardship". It is found only here and in 2:3 in the New Testament. The simple verb comes in 2:9 ("I am suffering hard things") and 4:5 ("put up with hardship"). The idea is not to seek suffering but to share in the hardship the good news brings, as Paul does. It is the first of the letter's many "with" words: died with, live with, reign with (2:11-12).

a: he did not go by what we had done
t: Saved by grace, not by works
p: God saved and called us by his own purpose and grace, not because of our works.
b: The Greek says "not according to our works". This is the same teaching found in Ephesians 2:8-9 and Titus 3:5, and a short form of Romans 3-4: salvation is God's free gift. Paul's undisputed letters speak of "works of the law"; the Pastorals speak more broadly of "works", and readers who see them as later letters say the debate over the Jewish law has faded into the background. The grace was given "in Christ Jesus" before time, so it does not depend on anything a person does. Churches agree that grace comes first; they differ on how faith, baptism and good works fit after it (see the topic page).

a: before the long ages of time
p: The Greek is "before times eternal": before the ages of the world began.
b: Pro chronon aionion means literally "before age-long times". Titus 1:2 has the same phrase for God's promise of eternal life. The point is that God's plan of grace is older than the world, as Ephesians 1:4 says: "he chose us in Christ before the world was founded". The grace was "given to us in Christ Jesus" before we existed, which shows that it is a gift held in Christ, not earned by us.

a: the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus
p: The Pastorals call Christ's coming his "appearing" (epiphaneia). Here it means his first coming; in 4:1, 8 his return.
b: Epiphaneia was the Greek word for a god showing himself to help his people, or for a ruler's grand arrival. The Pastoral Letters use it where Paul elsewhere uses parousia, "coming". In this verse the appearing is Christ's first coming, his life, death and rising, by which God's grace "has been brought into the open". In 4:1 and 4:8 the same word means his appearing at the end, and Titus 2:11-13 has both appearings side by side. "Savior" (soter) was also a title of gods and emperors. Calling Jesus "our Savior" and speaking of his "appearing" quietly claims for him what the Roman world gave to its rulers.

p: "Immortality" here is the Greek for "incorruption", life that does not rot or decay.
b: The Greek aphtharsia means "incorruption", not being subject to decay. Paul uses it for the resurrection body: "This thing that decays has to put on what cannot decay" (1 Corinthians 15:53). The two words "life and incorruption" may be one idea, "life that cannot decay". Christ "has made death powerless" (the verb katargeo, "make ineffective, put out of action"): death still happens, but it has lost its hold, as 1 Corinthians 15:26 says of the last enemy. The words matter in a letter written by a man who expects to die soon (4:6).

p: A herald (keryx) was the official who announced a ruler's message in public.
b: In Greek cities the keryx called out the decisions of the assembly, the start of games and the orders of a king. Paul uses the verb "proclaim as a herald" often (Romans 10:14-15), and in 4:2 he tells Timothy to "proclaim the word" with the same verb. 1 Timothy 2:7 gives Paul the same titles: herald, apostle and teacher of the Gentiles. On the words "of the Gentiles", found in some manuscripts here, see the variant.

p: The Greek says "my deposit". It can mean what Paul has entrusted to God, or what God has entrusted to Paul.
b: Paratheke was a legal and banking word: property left in someone's care, to be returned intact. "My deposit" is open. (1) It is what Paul has entrusted to God: his life, his work, his future, which God will keep safe "until that day". Many older English versions read it this way. (2) It is what God has entrusted to Paul: the good news, which God will protect even when Paul dies. The other two uses favor this second sense, since in 1:14 Timothy must "keep the good deposit safe", and in 1 Timothy 6:20 "guard the deposit" means the teaching. The Plain keeps "my deposit" so that both readings stay open; Paul's trust is in "the one I have put my trust in" either way.

p: "That day" is the day Christ appears to judge. The letter uses the phrase three times.
b: The phrase "that day" comes in 1:12, 1:18 and 4:8. It goes back to the prophets' "day of the LORD", the day God acts to judge and to save, which the New Testament applies to Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 1 Corinthians 3:13). In this letter the day is the time of reward, not of fear: mercy for Onesiphorus (1:18) and a crown for Paul and for all who have loved Christ's appearing (4:8).

p: The Pastorals call true teaching "sound", literally "healthy". The opposite is teaching that spreads like a disease (2:17).
b: The verb hygiaino means "to be in good health" (the root of English "hygiene"). The Pastoral Letters use it for teaching that is true and does people good: "sound teaching" (4:3; 1 Timothy 1:10; Titus 1:9), "sound words" (here and 1 Timothy 6:3). The image fits the opponents' talk, which "will eat its way like gangrene" (2:17). The word for "model" (hypotyposis) is a sketch or pattern to copy, as in 1 Timothy 1:16.

a: who has made his home in us
t: The Spirit who lives in believers
p: Timothy is not left to guard the teaching alone. The Holy Spirit who lives in "us" guards it with him.
b: The verb enoikeo, "live in, make a home in", is the same Paul uses in Romans 8:11 of "his Spirit who lives in you". In 1:5 the same verb says faith "made its home" first in Lois and Eunice. The "us" is broad: the Spirit lives in Paul, in Timothy and in the church, which is why the deposit can be kept after Paul dies.

a: all those in Asia turned their backs on me
p: Asia here is the Roman province in what is now western Turkey, with Ephesus as its leading city.
b: "Asia" in the New Testament means the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, where Paul had worked for years: "everyone living in Asia heard the Lord's word" (Acts 19:10). Now "all" in Asia have turned away from him. The "all" is probably an overstatement of grief, since Onesiphorus, from the same region, did not (1:16-18). It may mean that believers from Asia who could have spoken for him at his trial in Rome did not, or that churches of the province turned against his teaching. The letter does not say which. Phygelus and Hermogenes are named only here, and nothing more is known of them from the Bible.

p: Paul prays for Onesiphorus' household and for Onesiphorus himself "on that day". Some readers think he had died.
b: Paul wishes mercy on "the household of Onesiphorus" (here and 4:19), not on Onesiphorus himself, and in 1:18 he prays that Onesiphorus will "find mercy from the Lord on that day". One reading holds that Onesiphorus had died, perhaps after visiting Paul in Rome. If so, 1:18 is a prayer for a dead man, and Catholic and Orthodox writers have cited it in support of praying for the dead. Others reply that he may simply have been away from home when the letter was written, so that his household is greeted in his absence, and that a wish for mercy on the last day can be made for the living. The text does not say. See the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter page.

p: Paul speaks of his "chain", in the singular, as he does in Acts 28:20 and Ephesians 6:20.
b: A Roman prisoner in custody could be chained to a soldier. In Rome Paul told the Jewish leaders, "This chain is around me on account of Israel's hope" (Acts 28:20), and Ephesians 6:20 calls him "an ambassador in a chain". Visiting a prisoner was risky and shameful: it linked the visitor with a man accused of a crime. That is why Paul praises Onesiphorus because "my chain did not shame him".

p: Onesiphorus had to search hard to find Paul. That fits a prisoner held more strictly than in Acts 28.
b: In Acts 28:30 Paul lived "in quarters he paid for himself" and welcomed visitors, so he would not have been hard to find. Here a friend from Asia searches Rome "eagerly until he found me". Those who hold that Paul wrote the letter in a second, harsher imprisonment (the view of Eusebius, Church History 2.22) find support here. Others place the letter in the custody of Acts 28 and think the search was simply to find which of Rome's many prisons or houses held him. Those who think the letter is later than Paul read the scene as a picture of loyalty set against the desertions of 1:15.

a: May the Lord let him find mercy from the Lord
p: The double "Lord" probably means Christ grants mercy from God the Father, or simply repeats God's name.
b: The Greek has kyrios twice. Readers take it in two ways. (1) The first "Lord" is Christ, the judge on "that day" (4:8), and the second is God, from whom mercy comes. (2) It is a Jewish way of speaking that repeats the name for weight, as the Greek of Genesis 19:24 says the Lord rained fire "from the Lord". There is a play on words too: Onesiphorus searched and "found" Paul (1:17), and now Paul prays that he will "find" mercy.
orig: δῴη αὐτῷ ὁ κύριος εὑρεῖν ἔλεος παρὰ κυρίου (doe auto ho kyrios heurein eleos para kyriou)

p: Onesiphorus' service in Ephesus was known to Timothy, who seems to be there or nearby.
b: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia and the place where Paul worked longest (Acts 19:10; 20:31). 1 Timothy 1:3 pictures Timothy left there to lead the church. In 4:12 Paul has sent Tychicus to Ephesus, and in 4:19 he greets Onesiphorus' household and Prisca and Aquila, who had lived there (Acts 18:19, 26). So the letter's first readers are most naturally placed in or near Ephesus.

p: The Greek is passive: "be strengthened". The strength comes from grace, not from Timothy himself.
b: Endynamou is a command in the passive voice: "be made strong", "let yourself be strengthened". The same verb comes in 4:17: "the Lord ... made me strong". Paul asks Timothy to draw on a power he does not supply. Ephesians 6:10 uses the verb in the same way: "be made strong in the Lord".

p: Timothy heard Paul "through many witnesses": in front of them, or backed by them.
b: Dia pollon martyron is unusual, and the Plain keeps the literal "through" so as not to choose. Two readings are given. (1) "In the presence of many witnesses": a public occasion, perhaps Timothy's baptism or his being set apart; 1 Timothy 6:12 speaks of the good confession Timothy made "before many witnesses". (2) "Through", in the sense of "with the backing of": what Timothy heard from Paul was confirmed by many other witnesses, so it was not Paul's private teaching. Either way, the teaching was public and could be checked, unlike the "myths" of 4:4.

p: Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful people, they to others: a chain of teaching, each link holding a deposit.
b: The verb is paratithemi, "put in someone's keeping", from the same family as the "deposit" (paratheke) of 1:12, 14; the Plain says "entrust" to keep that link: what was put into Timothy's keeping is to be put into the keeping of others. The teaching is to go from Paul to Timothy, from Timothy to faithful people, and from them to others. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican readers have seen in this verse a picture of the succession of teachers and bishops from the apostles, a link that Irenaeus (about AD 180) drew when he traced the bishops of Rome from the apostles and noted, "Of this Linus, Paul makes mention in the Epistles to Timothy" (Against Heresies 3.3.3; compare 4:21). Many Protestant readers see a succession of faithful teaching, handed on by teachers who are tested, without a necessary chain of ordinations. Readers who date the letter after Paul see in it the second generation's concern to keep the apostle's teaching. See the card on this chapter page.

p: The Greek word here (anthropoi) means human beings, not males in particular.
b: Paul uses anthropois, the general word for human beings, not andrasin, "males". Many older English Bibles say "faithful men". Whether in practice the teachers Paul has in mind are all men is a separate question tied to 1 Timothy 2:12, which the topic "Women in Church Leadership" discusses. The Plain says "people" because that is what the word means.

t: The soldier, the athlete, the farmer
p: Three pictures follow, each about hard work and its reward: the soldier, the athlete, the farmer.
b: Paul often draws on these three figures, and he uses all three in 1 Corinthians 9:7, 24-25 when he speaks about his right to support. Here they teach endurance. The soldier gives his whole attention to the one who enlisted him (2:4). The athlete wins only if he keeps the rules (2:5). The farmer works first and then eats (2:6). Paul calls Epaphroditus a "fellow soldier" (Philippians 2:25) and Archippus too (Philemon 1:2), and 1 Timothy 1:18 tells Timothy to wage a good campaign. The military picture is not a call to violence: the "weapons" in Paul are truth, faith and the word (Ephesians 6:10-17).

a: the officer who signed him up
p: A Roman soldier was enrolled by an officer and owed him his whole service.
b: Stratologeo means "to enlist soldiers". The soldier on active service (strateuomenos) does not get "tangled up" (emplekomai) in the ordinary business (pragmateiai, trade and affairs) of civilian life. The point is focus, not that a Christian leader may never earn a living: Paul himself worked with his hands (Acts 18:3; 1 Thessalonians 2:9). The same verb "get tangled" is used in 2 Peter 2:20 of people caught again in the world's corruption.

a: he does not win the crown
p: A winner at the Greek games received a wreath, a "crown" of leaves, if he kept the rules.
b: The verb athleo means to compete in the games, and the "crown" (stephanos) was the wreath given to the winner. Breaking the rules meant losing the prize. "If he keeps the rules" (nomimos, "lawfully") points to the rules of the contest. Paul used the same picture to the Corinthians: "They do it to receive a crown that fades. We do it for one that never fades" (1 Corinthians 9:25). The picture comes back at the letter's end, with "the crown of righteousness" (4:8).

p: The farmer who does the work eats first. The point may be reward in the end, or the right of workers to be supported.
b: Two readings. (1) The picture is about reward: hard work now, harvest later, as with the soldier's and the athlete's prize. (2) The picture is about a worker's right to live from his work, as in 1 Corinthians 9:7, 10 and 1 Timothy 5:17-18, where Paul applies "Do not muzzle an ox" to leaders. Some readers also note the order: "first" the farmer must work hard, and only then share in the crop. Paul adds "Think about what I am saying" (2:7), which suggests the pictures need thought to apply.

p: Two short lines sum up the good news: Jesus was raised from the dead, and he was descended from David.
b: The pairing recalls the creed-like opening of Romans: "It is about his Son, who, according to the flesh, came from the offspring of David" (Romans 1:3), and "marked out as Son of God with power by his resurrection from the dead" (Romans 1:4). Many scholars think both passages echo an early Christian confession. "From the offspring (seed) of David" ties Jesus to God's promise to David of a son whose kingdom would last (2 Samuel 7:12-16). Reminding a prisoner's friend that Jesus himself was "raised from the dead" sets the frame for the suffering in the next verse.

p: Paul calls it "my good news": the message he preaches, not a different gospel of his own.
b: The phrase kata to euangelion mou appears also in Romans 2:16 and Romans 16:25. It does not mean Paul had a private gospel; it means "the good news as I preach it". This site writes "the good news" for euangelion, the word behind "gospel": the announcement of a victory or of a new king, which Paul applies to Jesus' death and resurrection.
orig: κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν μου (kata to euangelion mou)

a: like someone who has done evil
p: The word kakourgos, "evildoer", is the word Luke uses for the two criminals crucified with Jesus.
b: Kakourgos means "one who does evil", a criminal. Luke uses it for the men crucified on either side of Jesus (Luke 23:32-33, 39). The charge against Paul is not named. The point is the shame: the herald of the good news is treated like a common criminal. Tacitus, writing about Nero's persecution after the fire of AD 64, says the Christians were treated as "a class hated for their abominations" (Annals 15.44).

a: But God's word is not in chains
p: Paul is chained, but God's word is not. Acts ends on the same note.
b: The contrast is between Paul's chains and the word's freedom. The last words of Acts say the same of Paul in Rome: "with complete freedom to speak, and no one stopped him" (Acts 28:31). Philippians 1:12-14 says that Paul's imprisonment helped the good news spread. In this letter the point is practical: Timothy and the "faithful people" of 2:2 will carry the word after Paul is gone.

p: "The elect" (eklektoi) are those God has chosen. Paul endures so that they may reach salvation.
b: The Greek eklektoi, "chosen ones", is the word behind "the elect" in older English. Paul endures "for the sake of" them, "so that they too can reach the salvation". This is a puzzle for some readers: if God has chosen them, why must Paul suffer for them to be saved? One answer is that God uses the preaching and suffering of his servants to bring the chosen to faith. Another takes "the chosen" as the church as a body, God's people in Christ, which individuals join by faith and from which they can fall (2:12). The topic page on election sets out the views.

p: The Pastorals use this formula five times. Here it points to the lines that follow, which sound like an early hymn.
b: Pistos ho logos appears in 1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; Titus 3:8 and here. Each time it marks a saying the churches knew. Here it probably points forward to the four "if" lines of 2:11-13, which have a rhythm and balance that many scholars take as a quoted hymn or baptismal confession. Some think it points back to 2:8-10. The "for" (gar) that begins the next line in the Greek is often part of the quotation and is left out in the Plain.

t: Died with him: in baptism or in martyrdom?
p: The first line echoes Romans 6:8. It may mean dying with Christ in baptism, or dying for him as a martyr.
b: Romans 6:8 says, "If we died with Christ, we believe that we will live with him as well", and there the dying is in baptism (Romans 6:3-4). The Greek verb here is a past tense, "if we died with him", which fits a baptismal confession. But in a letter written from prison by a man about to die (4:6), many readers hear it of martyrdom as well. Both readings have long histories, and they need not exclude each other.

a: we will also reign with him
p: Those who endure will share Christ's rule as king. Revelation uses the same promise.
b: The verb symbasileuo means "rule as king together with". Paul uses the simple verb in Romans 5:17: those who receive grace will "rule in life through the one person, Jesus Christ". Revelation promises that the faithful will reign with Christ (Revelation 5:10; 20:4-6; 22:5). The line ties reigning to enduring now, which suits a letter about suffering.

a: he will deny us as well
p: This line echoes a saying of Jesus: whoever denies him before people, he will deny before his Father.
b: The Gospels have the saying: "But whoever denies me in front of people, I too will deny that person in front of my Father in heaven" (Matthew 10:33), and "But whoever denies me in front of people will be denied in front of God's angels" (Luke 12:9). The hymn turns it into a warning for believers under pressure. The Greek future, "if we will deny" (the critical text), may point to a final denial at a trial; the Byzantine text has the present, "if we deny", which makes no difference in English.

p: After "he will deny us", the last line says he stays faithful even when we are not. Readers argue over whether this is comfort or a warning.
b: The fourth line breaks the pattern: we are unfaithful, but he does not answer in kind. (1) Many read it as comfort: Christ keeps his promises to his people even when their faith fails, as Peter's denial was followed by his restoration. (2) Others read it as the other side of the warning: Christ stays true to himself, so he must keep his word, including the warning of 2:12. (3) Some combine the two: lapses of faith ("unfaithful", apisteo, which can also mean "do not believe") are different from final denial. "He cannot deny himself" means that God cannot act against his own nature (compare Titus 1:2, where God is the one who does not lie). The card on this page sets out how the churches answer the question of falling away.

p: The verb logomacheo means "fight about words". The Pastorals warn against it more than once.
b: Logomacheo, "to battle over words", occurs only here in the New Testament, and its noun is in 1 Timothy 6:4. The warning is not against careful thought; it is against arguments that only divide and "tear down those who are listening" (katastrophe, "overturning", the root of English "catastrophe"). The next verse gives the contrast: handling "the word of truth" straight.

a: cuts the word of truth straight
p: Orthotomeo means "cut straight", used in the Greek Proverbs of a straight road. The KJV has "rightly dividing".
b: Orthotomeo joins "straight" to "cut". In the Greek Proverbs it is used of paths: wisdom will "make your ways straight" (Proverbs 3:6 and 11:5 in the Septuagint). So many take it as "cutting a straight road" for the word, teaching it without detours. Others think of a stonemason or a farmer cutting a straight furrow, or of a priest dividing a sacrifice. The KJV's "rightly dividing the word of truth" has been taken by some teachers, Dispensationalists among them, as dividing Scripture into periods (dispensations); the Greek word does not mean that. The sense is clear enough: teach the true message accurately.

p: Dokimos means tested and found genuine, like a coin or metal that passes the test.
b: Dokimos was used of coins and metals tested and found genuine. A worker "tested and approved" by God has passed God's inspection. Its opposite is adokimos, "failed the test", which the letter uses of the false teachers (3:8). The worker who is not ashamed (anepaischyntos) echoes the letter's theme of shame (1:8, 12, 16).

p: Gangraina was the medical word for flesh that rots and spreads. The image is the opposite of "sound", healthy teaching.
b: Gangraina is decay that eats into healthy flesh, the word behind English "gangrene". The Greek says the talk "will have pasture" (nomen hexei): it will feed and spread. The picture fits the Pastorals' language of "sound" (healthy) teaching (1:13; 4:3): false teaching is a disease that spreads from person to person.

p: Hymenaeus is also named in 1 Timothy 1:20. Philetus appears only here.
b: In 1 Timothy 1:20 Paul says he handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan so that they would learn not to blaspheme. If it is the same man, the discipline did not stop him. Philetus is otherwise unknown. Their teaching is named in the next verse: the resurrection has already happened.

a: the resurrection has already taken place
p: These teachers said the resurrection was past, perhaps meaning a spiritual rising at baptism with no future bodily resurrection.
b: The letter does not explain the claim. The most common reading is that they took the resurrection to be spiritual: believers rose with Christ at baptism (compare Colossians 2:12; Ephesians 2:6), so there was no future rising of the body. In Corinth some said "no resurrection of the dead exists" (1 Corinthians 15:12), perhaps for a similar reason. Paul's letters do speak of being raised with Christ now, but always with a future resurrection still to come (Romans 6:5; Philippians 3:20-21). Some scholars connect the teaching with Greek ideas that the body is worthless, and with later Christian groups that held similar views.

a: The Lord knows the ones who are his
p: The first line of the "seal" comes from Numbers 16:5 in the Greek, Moses' answer to Korah's revolt.
b: When Korah and his band rebelled against Moses and Aaron, Moses said, "In the morning the LORD will make known who is his and who is holy" (Numbers 16:5). The Greek of Numbers reads egno ho theos tous ontas autou, "God knew those who are his"; 2 Timothy has "the Lord" (kyrios). The choice fits: like Korah, the false teachers of 2:17-18 have risen against God's appointed teachers, and God knows who really belongs to him. In Numbers Moses then told the people, "Turn away, please, from the tents of these wicked men" (Numbers 16:26), which may be behind the second line.

t: Where does the second line come from?
p: No Old Testament verse says exactly this. It seems to combine phrases from the Greek Bible.
b: The second line does not quote one verse. Its phrases are found in the Septuagint: "the one who names the name of the Lord" (Leviticus 24:16, Septuagint), "we name your name" (Isaiah 26:13, Septuagint), and "turn away from wrongdoing" (Sirach 17:26, a deuterocanonical book, Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians). Numbers 16:26, where Moses tells the people to turn away from the rebels' tents, may supply the idea. To "name the Lord's name" means to call on him, to confess him as one's Lord. Whoever does that must also live a clean life.

p: A seal marks ownership and authenticity. God's foundation bears an inscription with two sayings.
b: The "solid foundation" may be the church (1 Timothy 3:15 calls it the pillar and foundation of the truth), or God's saving work, or the true teaching. Builders sometimes carved an inscription on a foundation stone, and a seal stamped a document as genuine and as someone's property. Here the seal has two sides: God's choice ("The Lord knows the ones who are his") and human responsibility ("Everyone who speaks the Lord's name must keep away from wrongdoing"). Readers have often seen in the pair the balance of the whole letter.

p: In a big house some vessels are for special use and some for ordinary or dirty work. Romans 9:21 uses the same words.
b: A large household had fine gold and silver dishes and cheap wooden and clay ones, some for banquets and some for waste. Paul used the same words in another argument: "From one lump of clay, does the potter not have the authority to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?" (Romans 9:21). There God is the potter who decides; here the point is different, since 2:21 says a person can "scrub himself clean" and become a vessel for honor. Readers take the "house" as the church, where true and false teachers live side by side for now.

p: "These" may be the dishonorable vessels (the false teachers) or the wrong teachings and ways named before.
b: The verb ekkathairo means "clean out thoroughly". "These" has no clear noun. (1) It is the "vessels for dishonor", the false teachers: Timothy should keep apart from them. (2) It is the things named in 2:16-19: empty talk, false teaching, wrongdoing. Either way, the image moves from the house owner's choice to the vessel's own action, which suits the call to "keep away from wrongdoing" in 2:19. The "Master" (despotes, the owner of a household and its slaves) is God or Christ.
orig: ἐκκαθάρῃ ἑαυτὸν ἀπὸ τούτων (ekkathare heauton apo touton)

a: the desires that young people have
p: The phrase is not only about sex. In context it may mean the young man's love of argument, novelty and quick anger.
b: Neoterikai epithymiai are "desires of the young". Many readers think first of sexual desire, but the setting is about quarrels (2:14, 23-24). Some commentators suggest impatience, love of winning arguments, the craving for new ideas, or harshness, all faults of a young leader. Timothy was young (1 Timothy 4:12). "Run away" is the same verb as in 1 Corinthians 6:18 and 1 Timothy 6:11.

p: The Greek doulos means "slave". This site uses "slave" so that the force of the word is not softened.
b: Doulos is the ordinary Greek word for a slave. Paul calls himself "a slave of Christ Jesus" (Romans 1:1; Titus 1:1 "a slave of God"). In the Greek Old Testament "slave/servant of the Lord" is the title of Moses (Joshua 1:1), of David and of the prophets. The phrase is an honor as well as a description of total belonging. Here it describes how a church leader acts: like a servant in God's household, not a fighter.

a: Perhaps God will grant them repentance
p: Repentance is something God gives. Timothy's task is to teach gently and leave the change of heart to God.
b: "Repentance" (metanoia) is a change of mind and life: "turn your life around". Here, as in Acts 11:18 ("God has given even the Gentiles repentance that brings life!"), it is God's gift. Augustine and the Reformed tradition stress this: people do not turn to God unless God turns them. Others, in the Wesleyan and Arminian traditions, stress that God gives the grace to repent but people can refuse it. The verse joins both sides: God grants, and the opponents must "sober up" (2:26). Timothy's part is to correct "with a mild spirit".

a: where he had caught them alive to do his will
p: Greek uses two different words for "him" and "his". Caught by the devil for his will, or freed to do God's will?
b: The Greek is ezogremenoi hyp' autou eis to ekeinou thelema, "caught alive by him (autou) for that one's (ekeinou) will". Three readings: (1) caught by the devil to do the devil's will (most English versions); (2) caught by the devil, but now set free to do God's will; (3) caught alive by God's servant (2:24) to do God's will. The change of pronoun is what makes (2) and (3) possible. The verb zogreo means "take alive"; Luke 5:10 uses it when Jesus tells Simon, "From now on it is people you will be catching alive." The Plain keeps "his" so the reader can see the question.
orig: ἐζωγρημένοι ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ ἐκείνου θέλημα

p: The verb means "become sober again", as from drunkenness. False teaching is pictured as a stupor.
b: Ananepho means "return to sobriety". It is found only here in the New Testament. The picture is of people drugged or drunk, who wake to find themselves in a trap. Compare the call to "stay clear-headed" (nepho) in 4:5.

t: Are the last days now or later?
p: The "last days" may be a time still to come, or the time the church already lives in. Timothy is told to deal with these people now.
b: In the prophets "the latter days" meant the time when God would act at last. The New Testament says that time began with Jesus and the Spirit: at Pentecost Peter quotes Joel, "This is what will happen in the last days" (Acts 2:17), and Hebrews 1:2 says God has spoken "in these last days" by a Son. Here the future tense ("hard times will set in") sounds like a prediction, but 3:5 tells Timothy to "turn away from people like that", and 3:6-9 describes people already at work. So one reading takes the warning as describing Timothy's own time, seen as the last days. Another reads it as a prophecy for the time just before Christ returns, with Timothy's opponents as a first taste.

a: in love with themselves and in love with money
p: The list of vices begins with lovers of self and of money and ends with lovers of pleasure rather than of God.
b: The Greek list begins with two "lover" words (philautoi, "self-lovers", philargyroi, "money-lovers") and ends with two more (philedonoi, "pleasure-lovers", rather than philotheoi, "God-lovers", 3:4). The frame shows the root of every vice between: love turned away from God to self. The list has eighteen items, many of which also appear in the list in Romans 1:29-31 ("they are insolent, proud and boastful ... and they disobey their parents", Romans 1:30). Lists of vices were common in Greek moral writing and in Jewish writings of the time. 1 Timothy 6:10 calls the love of money a root of all kinds of evil.

p: The word for "slanderers" is diaboloi, the same word that, with "the", names the devil.
b: Diabolos means "slanderer, accuser". With the article, ho diabolos, it is "the devil", the accuser (2:26). Without the article it is used of people who slander (1 Timothy 3:11; Titus 2:3). The word "heartless" (astorgoi) means without the natural love of family; it is missing in Codex Sinaiticus as Tischendorf prints it, but it is in all the printed editions.

p: Godliness (eusebeia) was the Greek virtue of reverence for the gods, family and city. These people keep its outward form.
b: Eusebeia, "godliness", is a key word of the Pastoral Letters (1 Timothy 2:2; 3:16; 6:6; Titus 1:1). In ordinary Greek it meant proper reverence toward the gods, parents and city: a respected public virtue. The letters fill it with Christian content, reverence for God lived out in daily life. Morphosis is the outward form or outline of a thing; in Romans 2:20 it is "the very form of knowledge and truth" in the law. These people keep the shape and the words but "have said no to its power", the power of 1:7-8. "Turn away" shows Paul has present people in mind.

p: The Greek uses a scornful diminutive, "little women". Who they were, and what the passage says about women, is debated.
b: Gynaikaria is the diminutive of "woman", used in Greek with contempt: "silly little women". The verse describes some women in the households of the church, weighed down by sins and driven by desires, whom the false teachers "make captives". It does not say all women are like this; the letter honors Lois and Eunice (1:5) and greets Prisca (4:19) and Claudia (4:21). Readers differ on the setting. Some see the teachers going house to house to reach women who were kept at home and had little teaching, so that the fault lay with the teachers who exploited them. Some connect it with 1 Timothy 5:13, which speaks of younger widows going from house to house. Some feminist scholars point to the scornful word as a sign of how the writer viewed women who listened to rival teachers, and to the letter's general concern for households and good order. The topic "Women in Church Leadership" discusses the wider question.

p: The first churches met in homes, so teachers moved from house to house. The verb means to worm one's way in.
b: Endyno means to slip or creep in. The churches met in households (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19), and teachers who traveled could find hearers in one home after another, where the household head's welcome mattered. Titus 1:11 says false teachers were "turning whole households upside down". "Make captives" (aichmalotizo) is a war word, "take prisoner".
orig: ἐνδύνοντες εἰς τὰς οἰκίας (endynontes eis tas oikias)

p: Exodus does not name Pharaoh's magicians. Jewish tradition did: the names are in the Damascus Document, the Targum and the Talmud.
b: Exodus 7:11 says only that "the magicians of Egypt did the same with their spells". Jewish tradition gave them names. The Damascus Document from the Qumran sect (CD 5:17-19) says that when Moses and Aaron arose, Belial "raised up Yannes and his brother" (in E. Cook's translation; Davies' translation reads the name as "Yohanah", a form close to the Talmud's "Yohana"). The Aramaic paraphrase called Targum Pseudo-Jonathan names "Jannes and Jambres" as Pharaoh's chief magicians (on Exodus 1:15 and 7:11) and as Balaam's two young servants (Numbers 22:22). The Babylonian Talmud has "Yohana and Mamre" mocking Moses (Menachot 85a). Even the Roman writer Pliny the Elder named Jannes with Moses as founders of a school of magic (Natural History 30.2). Origen, in the 200s, says that there was an apocryphal book called The Book of Jannes and Jambres; Greek fragments of a book about the two survive in the Chester Beatty Papyri. Since the names were so widely known, Paul seems to draw on a story his readers knew, though the letter does not say where he learned it. The point of the comparison: like the magicians who copied Moses' signs, the false teachers imitate the truth but cannot match it.

a: just as the stupidity of those two became clear
p: In Exodus the magicians copied the first signs but failed at the gnats and admitted, "It is the finger of God".
b: The magicians matched the staff, the blood and the frogs (Exodus 7:11-12, 22; 8:7), but they could not make gnats, and they told Pharaoh it was God's finger (Exodus 8:18-19); later they could not even stand before Moses because of the boils (Exodus 9:11). The letter promises the same end for the false teachers: they can imitate for a while, but their folly (anoia, "mindlessness") will be plain to all.

a: You, though, have kept close to me
p: Parakoloutheo means to follow closely, to know thoroughly by following along. Timothy knows Paul's life from the inside.
b: The verb was used of a disciple who follows a teacher, and of someone who has investigated a matter closely (Luke 1:3 uses it of Luke's research). The list that follows mixes teaching with way of life and suffering: Timothy has seen not only what Paul taught but how he lived and what it cost. The contrast is with the opponents of 3:1-9, whose life does not match their show of godliness.

a: in Antioch, in Iconium, in Lystra
p: The three cities of Paul's first journey are where Timothy grew up. He may have seen Paul's sufferings there himself.
b: Acts tells of these persecutions on Paul's first journey: in Antioch of Pisidia the Jews "roused a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and threw them out of their territory" (Acts 13:50); in Iconium there was a plot to stone them (Acts 14:5); at Lystra "they talked the crowds around, pelted Paul with stones and hauled him outside the town" (Acts 14:19). Timothy was from Lystra and had a good name "among the brothers at Lystra and Iconium" (Acts 16:2), so he may have seen these things as a young man. The mention of the first journey rather than later troubles fits Timothy's own memories. "The Lord pulled me out" is the same verb as Psalm 34:4 in the Greek and 4:17-18 below.
r: Acts 13:50; Acts 14:5; Acts 14:19; Acts 16:1-2; 2 Corinthians 11:25; Psalm 34:4

p: Paul says everyone who wants to live in a godly way in Christ will be persecuted. Readers ask whether this is literal for every believer.
b: Acts records Paul and Barnabas telling the new disciples of these same cities, "We must go through many troubles to enter the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22). Jesus said the same (John 15:20). Some readers take the verse as a rule without exceptions, with "persecution" as any hostility or loss for faith. Others see a general truth for a church under pressure, like the first readers, without claiming that every believer in every age will suffer in the same way. Either way the verse sets Paul's suffering, and Timothy's, within what is normal for followers of Christ.

p: The word goes back to "sorcerer", and fits the mention of Pharaoh's magicians in 3:8.
b: Goes first meant a wailer of spells, a sorcerer, and then a cheat or impostor. After Jannes and Jambres in 3:8, the word keeps the picture of magicians in view: the false teachers do tricks with words. "Leading others astray and being led astray themselves" shows that they are deceived as well as deceivers.

p: "The holy writings" are the Jewish Scriptures Timothy learned as a child, probably in Greek. The New Testament did not yet exist.
b: Hiera grammata means "sacred letters" or "holy writings". What Timothy learned "from a small child" (brephos, a baby) was the Law, the Prophets and the other writings of Israel, read in a Jewish household in Asia Minor, probably in the Greek translation called the Septuagint. Whether that collection included books such as Sirach and Wisdom, which are in the Septuagint and later in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, is part of the debate about the canon: see the topic page. The point here is that these Scriptures can make a person wise "for salvation" when they are read "through the faith that is in Christ Jesus".

a: Every Scripture is God-breathed and useful
p: The Greek has no verb. It can be read "every Scripture is God-breathed and useful" or "every God-breathed Scripture is also useful".
b: The Greek is pasa graphe theopneustos kai ophelimos, literally "every scripture God-breathed and useful", with no "is". (1) Most translations supply "is" twice: "every (or all) Scripture is God-breathed and useful". The kai ("and") joining two adjectives favors this. (2) The American Standard Version of 1901 reads "Every scripture inspired of God is also profitable", taking "God-breathed" as describing which scriptures are meant. Both readings say that the Scriptures are God-breathed. Pasa without "the" usually means "every", each passage or each book, though "all" is also possible. The manuscripts agree in this clause: Codex Sinaiticus and all the editions read the same words. Later in the verse the Byzantine text has a different form of the word for "exposing wrong" (see the variant).
orig: πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος (pasa graphe theopneustos kai ophelimos)

p: Theopneustos means "breathed by God". It is the only use of the word in the Bible.
b: Theopneustos joins "God" to a form of the verb "breathe". English versions say "given by inspiration of God" (KJV), "inspired by God", "God-breathed" or "breathed out by God". The image recalls God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7) and the word of the LORD as his breath (Psalm 33:6). The verse says where Scripture comes from (God) and what it is for (teaching, correction, training); it does not explain how God and the human writers worked together. 2 Peter 1:21 adds that people "carried along by the Holy Spirit" spoke from God. The churches' teaching on inspiration, and on whether it means that Scripture is without error, is set out in the card on this chapter page and on the topic page.

p: When the letter was written, "Scripture" meant the Jewish Scriptures. How far the verse also covers the New Testament is a later question.
b: In the New Testament graphe, "writing, Scripture", nearly always means Israel's Scriptures, the "holy writings" of 3:15. Christians apply the verse to the New Testament too. Two passages show how that happened. 1 Timothy 5:18 introduces a saying found in Luke 10:7 alongside Deuteronomy 25:4 under "the Scripture says", and 2 Peter 3:16 puts Paul's letters next to "the other Scriptures". Readers who date the Pastorals late see these as signs that Christian writings were already being read as Scripture. Which books count as Scripture is answered differently by the churches: see the topic "How Books Got into the Bible".

a: for exposing wrong, for putting things right
p: Scripture is useful for teaching, for exposing wrong, for putting it right, and for training in righteousness: two for belief, two for life.
b: The four words are didaskalia (teaching), elegmos (exposing, rebuking, proving wrong), epanorthosis (setting upright again, correcting) and paideia (the training and discipline given to a child). Some readers see a pair for doctrine (teaching what is true, exposing what is false) and a pair for conduct (putting right what is wrong, training in what is right). The verb of elegmos returns in 4:2: "Expose wrong".
orig: πρὸς ἐλεγμόν, πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν (pros elegmon, pros epanorthosin)

p: The Greek is "the man of God", the Old Testament title of Moses, Elijah and the prophets.
b: Ho tou theou anthropos is the Greek Bible's phrase for "the man of God", used of Moses ("Moses the man of God", Deuteronomy 33:1), Elijah ("Man of God," 1 Kings 17:18) and other prophets. 1 Timothy 6:11 gives Timothy the same title, and the Plain uses the same words in both places so the link can be seen. So the verse may speak first of the church's leader, equipped by Scripture as the prophets were. But the word anthropos is the general word for a human being, not the word for a male (aner), and many read the verse of every believer: "the person of God". "Fully fit" and "equipped" (artios, exertismenos) are from one root: ready, fitted out.
orig: ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος (ho tou theou anthropos)

p: Diamartyromai means to declare solemnly before witnesses, under oath, as in court. God and Christ are the witnesses.
b: Diamartyromai is used of solemn testimony and charge with witnesses present. Paul uses the same verb in 2:14 and 1 Timothy 5:21. Here the witnesses are God and Christ Jesus, "who is about to judge the living and the dead": a phrase found also in Acts 10:42 ("to judge the living and the dead") and 1 Peter 4:5, and later in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds. The charge is made "by his appearing and by his kingdom", as one would swear by something sacred. The King James Version reads "at his appearing": see the variant.

a: when the time is right and when it is not
p: A play on words: eukairos, akairos, "timely, untimely". Be ready whether the moment seems right or not.
b: Eukairos akairos rhymes in Greek: "welcome or unwelcome", "timely or untimely". The KJV's "in season, out of season" became an English saying. Readers ask whose convenience is meant: the hearers' (speak even when they do not want to hear) or the speaker's (speak even when it is hard for you). The next verse suggests the first: a time is coming when people will not listen. The verbs "expose wrong, rebuke, urge on" pick up 3:16, and "with endless patience" keeps them from harshness, as in 2:24-25.

p: People with "itching ears" want to hear what pleases them, and they find teachers to scratch the itch.
b: Knethomenoi ten akoen, "having the hearing tickled", is a picture of people who want something pleasant and new for their ears. They "heap up" (episoreuo) teachers to suit their own cravings, a crowd of teachers instead of one truth. The contrast is with "sound", healthy teaching (1:13). The Old Testament knows the same problem: people who say to the prophets, "Tell us pleasant things" (Isaiah 30:10).

p: The Pastorals warn against "myths" (mythoi): stories and speculations that the writer sets against the truth.
b: Mythos meant a story, often a tale of the gods, and in philosophical writing a story set against reasoned truth. The Pastorals use it for the opponents' teaching: "myths and endless genealogies" (1 Timothy 1:4), "the kind of tales old women tell" (1 Timothy 4:7) and "Jewish myths" (Titus 1:14). What they were is debated: speculative retellings of Old Testament stories, early forms of Gnostic teaching about spiritual beings, or both. 2 Peter 1:16 uses the word in the same way.

p: An evangelist (euangelistes) is someone who tells the good news. Only Philip is called one in Acts.
b: The word appears only three times in the New Testament: Philip "the evangelist" (Acts 21:8), the gifts of Ephesians 4:11 ("some as evangelists"), and here. It may describe a role rather than a fixed office: carrying the good news to those who have not heard. Timothy is asked to do this work as well as to lead and teach the church. "Carry your ministry through to the end" (plerophoreo, "fully accomplish") uses the same verb as 4:17, "carried through in full".

a: a drink offering being poured out
t: Poured out as a drink offering
p: The verb means to be poured out as a libation, the wine poured beside a sacrifice. Paul sees his death as an offering to God.
b: Spendomai is the verb for pouring a drink offering. In the Law, wine was poured out with the daily offerings: "Pour out a drink offering of strong drink to the LORD in the holy place" (Numbers 28:7), and the Greek Bible's word for it is sponde. Philippians 2:17 uses the same verb, where Paul pictures his life poured out over the Philippians' faith. Here he says it is "already" happening: his death has begun. A Jewish reader would see his death as worship, not defeat. Greeks and Romans also poured libations to the gods, so the picture was clear to everyone.

a: the time for me to depart
p: Analysis, "departure", means a loosing or release. It is a gentle word for death.
b: Analysis means "loosing, release", and so "departure". Paul uses the verb in Philippians 1:23: "I long to leave and be with Christ". The image is of setting out on a journey, not of an ending. "Is here" (ephesteken) means the moment has arrived.

a: I have competed in the good contest
p: Agon is an athletic contest or struggle. The familiar "fought the good fight" makes it sound like a battle; the Greek pictures the games.
b: Ton kalon agona egonismai uses one root twice: "I have contested the good contest". Agon was a contest in the games, a race or a wrestling match, and by extension any hard struggle. The next line keeps to the games: "I have run the course (dromos, a race track) to the finish". 1 Timothy 6:12 has the same words as a command to Timothy. Paul said to the Ephesian elders, "if only I can finish my race and the service the Lord Jesus gave me" (Acts 20:24). The familiar English "fought the good fight" goes back to the King James Version's "I have fought a good fight".
orig: τὸν καλὸν ἀγῶνα ἠγώνισμαι (ton kalon agona egonismai)

t: Kept faith, or guarded the faith?
p: "I have kept the faith" can mean "I have stayed loyal" or "I have guarded the teaching entrusted to me".
b: Ten pistin teteraka can be read in two ways. (1) "I have kept faith": a common Greek phrase for keeping one's word, staying loyal to the end, as a soldier keeps faith with his commander. (2) "I have guarded the faith", the body of teaching, the "deposit" of 1:12-14. The letter's language of guarding the deposit favors (2); the athletic pictures around it suggest (1), the athlete who kept his oath to compete fairly. Both describe a life finished well.

t: What is the crown of righteousness?
p: The winner's wreath. It may be the crown that is righteousness, a reward for a righteous life, or one given by a just Judge.
b: The stephanos was the wreath given to the winner of a contest (2:5). "The crown of righteousness" can mean: (1) the crown that consists of righteousness, the final declaration that one is in the right with God (compare "the crown of life", James 1:12; Revelation 2:10); (2) the reward given for a righteous life; or (3) the crown given justly by "the Judge who is righteous". The churches have debated how such rewards relate to grace. Many point out that the crown is promised not only to Paul but to "all who have set their love on his appearing", which is not a reward for special achievement. The contrast with Paul's earthly judge, the emperor's court, is plain: the Lord is the Judge who is righteous.

a: all who have set their love on his appearing
p: The crown goes to all who have loved Christ's appearing, here his coming at the end.
b: The Greek perfect tense, "have loved", describes a settled love that has lasted until the day of reward. "Appearing" (epiphaneia) here means Christ's coming at the end, as in 4:1. The same verb "love" comes back in 4:10: Demas "loved the present age". The letter sets two loves side by side: love for Christ's appearing, and love for the present age.
orig: τοῖς ἠγαπηκόσι τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ (tois egapekosi ten epiphaneian autou)

p: Demas had been Paul's coworker. Now he has left, because he "loved the present age".
b: Demas is named among Paul's coworkers in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 1:24, with Luke and Mark. Here he has "left me behind" (enkataleipo, "abandon, desert"; the same verb in 4:16 and in the Greek of Psalm 22:1, "why have you abandoned me?"). The reason given is that he "loved the present age" (ton nyn aiona), the world as it is now, as opposed to the age to come. The letter does not say whether he gave up his faith or only gave up the danger of staying with a prisoner.

p: Crescens is named only here. Titus, Paul's coworker in Corinth and Crete, has gone to Dalmatia on the Adriatic coast.
b: Titus was a Greek coworker of Paul (Galatians 2:1, 3), sent to Corinth (2 Corinthians 8:23) and, according to the letter to him, left on Crete (Titus 1:5). Dalmatia was the southern part of the Roman province of Illyricum, on the east coast of the Adriatic Sea; Paul says he had preached "as far as Illyricum" (Romans 15:19). Unlike Demas, Crescens and Titus seem to have gone on assignments. On whether Crescens went to Galatia or to Gaul, see the variant.

a: Luke is the only one with me
p: Luke the doctor stayed with Paul. Eusebius used this verse in dating the book of Acts.
b: Luke is called the doctor in Colossians 4:14 and a coworker in Philemon 1:24. Tradition makes him the author of Luke and Acts, whose "we" passages place the writer with Paul on the voyage to Rome (Acts 27:1-28:16). Eusebius (Church History 2.22.6) noted that in this letter Luke was with Paul, "but at his first defense not even he", and concluded: "it is probable that Luke wrote the Acts of the Apostles at that time", that is, during Paul's first stay in Rome, where Acts ends. "Only" does not contradict the greetings of 4:21 from Christians in Rome: Luke is the only one of Paul's traveling companions still with him.

a: Pick up Mark and bring him along
p: Paul once refused to take Mark with him. Now he asks for him because Mark is "of great use".
b: John Mark had left Paul and Barnabas on their first journey, and Paul "did not think it fitting to take him along" on the second. "The quarrel became so heated that the two split up" (Acts 15:38-39). Colossians 4:10 and Philemon 1:24 show Mark with Paul again, and here Paul asks for him by name. The word "of great use" (euchrestos) is the same as in 2:21 ("of good use to the Master") and in Philemon 1:11, where Onesimus has become "useful". Many readers see here a friendship restored. Tradition connects Mark with the Gospel of Mark.

a: I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus
p: Tychicus, from Asia, was Paul's trusted messenger. He may be carrying this letter, or coming to replace Timothy.
b: Tychicus was "from Asia" and traveled with Paul (Acts 20:4). Ephesians 6:21 and Colossians 4:7 say he carried those letters and news of Paul. Titus 3:12 mentions sending him to Crete. "I have sent" may be the Greek letter-writer's past tense, meaning "I am sending" him with this letter, or it may mean he has already gone. Some think he was coming to take Timothy's place in Ephesus so that Timothy could come to Rome (4:9).

p: The phailones was a heavy traveling cape. With winter coming (4:21), a prisoner would need it.
b: The phailones (from the Latin paenula) was a heavy round cape with a hole for the head, worn in bad weather and on journeys. Paul had left it with Carpus in Troas, the port on the Asian coast from which ships crossed to Macedonia (Acts 16:8-11; 20:6). The request is very ordinary, and many readers find it hard to imagine a later writer inventing it; others reply that such details were a known part of letters written in someone's name. Among those who think a follower wrote the letter, some suggest that this and other personal notes came from real letters of Paul.

a: the scrolls too, especially the parchments
p: Paul asks for his "books" and especially his "parchments". The letter does not say what was in them.
b: Ta biblia are scrolls, usually of papyrus. Membranai is a Latin loanword for parchment, prepared animal skin, which could be made into notebooks. What they held is not said. Readers have suggested scrolls of the Scriptures, Paul's own notes or copies of his letters, or legal papers such as proof of his Roman citizenship. Some scholars connect the parchment notebooks with the early Christian habit of copying Scripture in bound books (codices) rather than scrolls, but the verse itself only shows that Paul valued them.
orig: τὰ βιβλία, μάλιστα τὰς μεμβράνας (ta biblia, malista tas membranas)

p: An Alexander is named in 1 Timothy 1:20 and in Ephesus in Acts 19:33. Whether they are the same man is unknown.
b: Alexander was a common name. 1 Timothy 1:20 names an Alexander with Hymenaeus as men Paul disciplined. Acts 19:33 tells of an Alexander pushed forward by the Jews during the riot of the silversmiths in Ephesus. This one is a chalkeus, a worker in copper or bronze, or any smith. He may have been an informer against Paul, since 4:15 warns that he "stood fiercely against our words" and Timothy should beware of him: so he was where Timothy would meet him.

t: Repaid by what he has done
p: The words echo Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12 in the Greek: God repays each one according to his works.
b: The Septuagint of Psalm 62:12 (61:13 in the Greek) says apodoseis hekasto kata ta erga autou, "you will repay each according to his works", with the same verb Paul uses. The site's Plain from the Hebrew reads "for you pay each person back by what he does" (Psalm 62:12), and Proverbs 24:12 "he will give every human being what his deeds deserve". Paul quotes the line in Romans 2:6: "He will pay back each person according to his works." The statement leaves judgment to God. Some later manuscripts turn it into a wish, "may the Lord pay him back": see the variant.

a: The first time I made my defense
p: Paul's "first defense" was probably the first hearing of his case in a Roman court. No one came to speak for him.
b: Apologia is a legal defense. A Roman trial could have a first hearing followed by a second. Most interpreters take this as the first hearing of the present case in Rome, after which the case was continued. Eusebius (Church History 2.22) read the verses as pointing to Paul's escape from danger in an earlier trial and to his later death under Nero. No one "came to my side" (paraginomai, to stand by as a supporter or advocate). The Lord did (4:17).
orig: ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ μου ἀπολογίᾳ (en te prote mou apologia)

a: May it not be held against them
p: Paul forgives those who abandoned him, as Stephen forgave those who stoned him.
b: Stephen died saying, "Lord, do not count this sin against them!" (Acts 7:60), and Jesus on the cross: "Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34). The verb logizomai, "reckon, count", is the same Paul uses in Romans 4 for God "reckoning" righteousness. Paul treats those who left him differently from Alexander (4:14): weakness is forgiven; active opposition is left to God's judgment.

t: Preaching to the nations at a trial
p: Paul's defense before a Roman court became a proclamation to the Gentile world, perhaps to Rome itself.
b: When Paul was called, the Lord said he would carry Christ's name "before Gentiles, before kings" (Acts 9:15). A defense in the capital before Roman officials was a chance to proclaim the message at the center of the Gentile world. Some readers take "all the Gentiles" as a broad way of saying the court in Rome, the capital of the nations; others as the climax of Paul's whole mission. The verb translated "reach its full extent" (plerophoreo, "fill to the full") is the one in 4:5, "carry your ministry through to the end".

a: I was pulled from the lion's mouth
p: "The lion's mouth" echoes Psalm 22:21. It means deadly danger, though some have taken it of Nero or of the arena.
b: Psalm 22, the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross, cries, "Save me from the lion's mouth!" (Psalm 22:21); the Greek of the psalm has the same words, "out of the mouth of a lion". Daniel was saved when God "sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths" (Daniel 6:22). Readers take the lion as: (1) a picture of mortal danger, the most common view; (2) the emperor Nero, as Eusebius took it (Church History 2.22); (3) Satan, the roaring lion of 1 Peter 5:8; or (4) literal lions in the arena. The rescue was from death at that time, not from all suffering: Paul still expects to die (4:6).

a: The Lord will pull me out of every evil work
p: Paul expects to die, yet says the Lord will rescue him. The rescue is from evil, and safety is for the kingdom in heaven.
b: Paul has just said he is being poured out (4:6), so the rescue he expects is not escape from death. It is rescue from "every evil work": from the harm of his enemies, from failing in faith, and from evil's final power. The words recall the Lord's Prayer, "rescue us from the evil one" (Matthew 6:13), with the same verb. "Keep me safe for his kingdom in heaven" (sosei eis, "will save into") means bringing him safely through death into the kingdom. The doxology that follows is the same as Galatians 1:5.

p: The couple who worked with Paul in Corinth, Ephesus and Rome. Paul calls her "Prisca"; Acts calls her "Priscilla".
b: Acts tells how Paul met Aquila and "his wife Priscilla", Jews expelled from Rome by Claudius, in Corinth (Acts 18:2), and how they went with him to Ephesus and taught Apollos there (Acts 18:18-26). Romans 16:3 greets them in Rome ("Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus"), and 1 Corinthians 16:19 sends their greetings from Ephesus with "the church that meets in their house". Here they are back in or near Ephesus. Prisca is named first four times out of six, which many readers take as a sign of her standing in the church. Paul uses the short form of her name, Prisca; Luke uses the diminutive Priscilla.

p: An Erastus traveled with Timothy (Acts 19:22), and an Erastus was city treasurer of Corinth (Romans 16:23).
b: Acts 19:22 says Paul sent "Timothy and Erastus" ahead into Macedonia from Ephesus. Romans, written from Corinth, sends greetings from "Erastus, the city treasurer" (Romans 16:23). It is possible that these are the same man, and that he stayed in his home city of Corinth; the name was not rare, so it is not certain.

a: Trophimus I left sick in Miletus
t: Trophimus left sick, and the route of Paul's travels
p: Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus. This visit does not easily fit the journeys in Acts, which is part of the authorship debate.
b: Trophimus was "from Asia" (Acts 20:4), "a man from Ephesus" (Acts 21:29). In Acts, Paul stopped at Miletus on his last journey to Jerusalem (Acts 20:15-17), but Trophimus went on with him to Jerusalem, where he was seen in the city (Acts 21:29), and Paul then went to Rome as a prisoner by way of Crete, not Miletus. So this verse points to a journey not told in Acts. Those who hold that Paul wrote the letter place it after a release from the imprisonment of Acts 28. Those who think a follower wrote the letter see one of the signs that the travel notes do not fit Paul's known life. The verse also shows that Paul did not heal every sick friend (compare 1 Timothy 5:23; Philippians 2:26-27).
r: Acts 20:4; Acts 20:15-17; Acts 21:29; Acts 27:7-8; Philippians 2:26-27; 1 Timothy 5:23

p: Sea travel nearly stopped in the winter months. If Timothy waited, he could not come until spring.
b: Ships on the Mediterranean avoided the open sea in winter. Acts shows the danger: "Going on by sea had become risky, since the Fast was already past" (Acts 27:9), and Paul's ship was wrecked. If Timothy did not come before winter he would have to wait months, and Paul did not expect to have months (4:6). The cloak of 4:13 fits the same season.

p: Irenaeus (about AD 180) names Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles and says Paul mentions him in the letters to Timothy.
b: Irenaeus, listing the bishops of Rome to show that their teaching came from the apostles, says that the apostles gave the office of bishop to Linus, and adds: "Of this Linus, Paul makes mention in the Epistles to Timothy" (Against Heresies 3.3.3). Anacletus and then Clement followed him. Historians debate how early Rome had a single bishop over all its house churches. Nothing else is known of Eubulus, Pudens or Claudia from the New Testament.

p: The Greek "brothers" (adelphoi) is used of the whole church family, women included. Claudia is named in the same verse.
b: Paul's word for fellow believers is adelphoi, "brothers". The plural was normal Greek for a mixed group, and here it follows the name of a woman, Claudia, among those sending greetings. This site writes "brothers", as in Acts and Romans, with the gloss "brothers and sisters".

p: The letter ends with "your spirit" (singular, Timothy) and then "with you" (plural): it was meant to be read to a church.
b: "The Lord be with your spirit" uses the singular "your": Timothy. "Grace be with you" uses the plural hymon, which English "you" cannot show. There is no "all" in the Greek here. 1 Timothy 6:21 and Titus 3:15 also end with a plural "you" (Titus adds "all"). Although the letter is addressed to one man, its last words show that it was expected to be read aloud in the church. Readers who think it was written after Paul's death see in the plural the real audience, the churches of the writer's time.
